title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM intent→configuration generator and an emulated execution reduces the proportion of configurations that would execute with operational faults. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification) we evaluated 72 preregistered paired intents with gpt-5-mini and a canonical deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed with 144 episodes (72 pairs) and 72 model calls. All baseline executions produced no emulator-observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected-fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics this degenerate confirmatory outcome is expected when identical generated candidates produce no baseline execution faults. We report deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, exact inferential outputs, and artifact-grounded methodological recommendations for designs that can measure verifier utility under realistic error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high-level operator intents into low-level device configurations for network operations (NetOps). This intent→configuration translation promises faster change pipelines but raises operational risk: a generated configuration can silently violate reachability, policy, or dependency-ordering invariants and cause outages if executed without further checks. A practical mitigation in deployment proposals is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that pairs stochastic LLM generation with deterministic verification and, when needed, repair or human review. Prior work demonstrates intent→configuration accuracy in constrained vendor dialects [1] and prototype co‑pilots that include verification components [2], but systematic, preregistered experiments that report verifier detection performance against executed outcomes remain scarce [3].

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment that isolates the verifier’s detection capability on identical generator outputs under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The central research question is: does inserting a deterministic network verifier between an LLM generator and emulator execution materially reduce the proportion of configurations that execute with operational faults when the identical generated candidate is evaluated both without and with verification? By design the experiment measures only deterministic detection on the same candidate, avoiding confounding due to generator sampling variability. Our empirical contribution is an artifact‑grounded, fully archived confirmatory run (72 paired intents) showing a ceiling outcome (zero baseline faults), plus methodological recommendations for future designs capable of measuring verifier utility.
sections.related_work:
Recent literature documents multiple strands relevant to LLM-driven NetOps. First, intent→configuration translation evaluations show promising task-level accuracy under constrained vendor dialects and emulator settings [1]. Second, multi-agent and tool‑augmented frameworks propose integrating validators into co‑pilot and agentic stacks, often without preregistered detection-evaluations tied to executed outcomes [2,4]. Third, generate–verify–repair architectures are established in code and software-repair research as a way to combine stochastic generation with deterministic checkers and iterative repair; adaptation to network semantics is an open empirical problem [3].

Classical deterministic network verification techniques (header-space analysis, reachability and policy checkers) provide precise invariants for forwarding-plane properties and ordering constraints; these methods are natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks [5]. However, the literature supplies limited direct experimental evidence coupling LLM generators, canonical verifiers, and end‑to‑end emulator execution with preregistered estimands. Our study situates a strict paired test—focused on verifier detection on identical candidates—within this gap and reports the artifact-grounded outcomes and practical implications.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 and froze the design before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). The confirmatory hypothesis H1 targeted an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 with two‑sided alpha = 0.05 and power ≥ 0.80; preregistered sample size was N = 72 paired intents stratified equally across three topology/difficulty strata (24 pairs per stratum).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract. Per the execution contract each intent received exactly one initial LLM generation shared across baseline and guarded conditions. Baseline: the shared candidate is executed in an isolated emulator and the outcome (fault/no fault) is recorded. Guarded: the deterministic verifier is run on the identical candidate; if it flags violations the guarded outcome is recorded as prevented (no emulator execution); if it does not flag, the same candidate is executed. This contract isolates verifier detection on identical outputs and prevents generator-sampling differences from influencing the paired comparison. Because only one shared candidate exists per intent, verifier benefits that depend on alternate sampling or repair are not attainable in this design.

Model and runtime parameters. The requested model was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). The provider was recorded as openai_responses and runtime sampling parameters are recorded in the archived model configuration; specifically, temperature is recorded as null, indicating provider-default sampling semantics were used at runtime rather than an explicit numerical temperature. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the canonical verifier used was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = "5.0"), implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule set that returns per‑episode validity and a structured validator_trace.

Task generation, constraints, and contamination controls. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry contains a structured natural-language intent, a required_sequence of field changes, allowed_touched_fields, initial and expected final states, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). The preregistration required exact‑match contamination checks against known public corpora; any exact match would be excluded. In the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded and contamination_summary recorded zero flagged contaminations.

Execution, retries, and deterministic accounting. The missingness plan permitted up to two additional retries for transient hosted-API errors. All retries and provider-call metadata were logged. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 144, completed_episode_count = 144, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 72 (one shared generation per pair). Provider-call audit confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 72 and cache_miss_count = 72, consistent with the preregistered shared_initial_generation stage.

Scoring and analysis. The verifier produces episode-level binary outcomes and detailed traces containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, difficulty metadata, normalized_configuration, validation_before/after final_state mappings, violation_codes, and violation_count. The primary analysis used the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor to construct a paired contingency table and to apply an exact McNemar two‑sided test when discordant pairs existed. We computed paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals for the paired difference with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed = 1729) to quantify uncertainty reproducibly. Pre-specified subgroup confirmatory comparisons (topology complexity and policy type) were recorded but remain noninformative given the observed ceiling outcome.
sections.results:
Execution and deterministic reconciliation. The run completed without technical failures. Key deterministic artifact counts: planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72. Deterministic_reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 72 and that all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Paired contingency and inferential outcomes. Aggregating across the preregistered 72 pairs yields contingency counts guarded×baseline: n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Condition summaries record baseline_success_count = 72 (success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 72 (success_rate = 1.0). The paired estimate paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]; the archive records the bootstrap seed and resamples. The contingency CSV and condition summary CSV are archived as analysis artifacts and reproduce the counts exactly.

Representative validator traces. Representative scoring artifacts for sample tasks (e.g., the first six task scoring JSONs in the archive) show validator_trace fields: parsed_command_count ranging 2–6, required_command_count matching task required_sequence lengths, difficulty.level marked medium/hard/very_hard, normalized_configuration matching the shared candidate, validator_version = "5.0", score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", and violation_count = 0. These traces confirm that the verifier parsed and validated each shared candidate and produced no violation flags for the preregistered task bank.

Missingness, exclusions, and contamination. analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 72 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero exact-match contaminations. Because there were no excluded pairs, the preregistered sensitivity analysis treating excluded items as failures did not alter the numerical conclusion.

Sensitivity diagnostics. The archived analysis log records bootstrap_resamples = 10000 and bootstrap_seed = 1729. Secondary and exploratory analyses (including subgroup inspections and the pre-specified Holm correction procedure) were executable but are non-informative because the contingency table contains no discordant pairs. All analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis_log.jsonl) are present in the archive and reproduce the reported numerical outputs.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling/null outcome. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate paired design validly isolates verifier detection on identical candidates. Observing zero baseline faults yields a scientifically informative ceiling/null outcome: under the chosen prompt/template, declared model (gpt-5-mini), and synthetic/emulated task bank the generator outputs were uniformly valid in the emulator and thus the verifier had no executed failures to prevent. The numeric outputs (n_11 = 72, p = 1.0, bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]) are direct consequences of the preregistration and observed data and do not imply that deterministic verifiers are unnecessary in general.

Design implications for measuring verifier utility. The shared_initial_candidate contract sacrifices sensitivity to verifier-mediated benefits that arise through repairs or alternate candidate selection. To measure operational utility of verifiers, future preregistered experiments should include one or more of: (1) independent-generation arms, where separate generator calls per condition permit verifier-influenced sampling differences; (2) repair-enabled flows, allowing a single deterministic repair call after a verifier flag and execution of the repaired candidate; (3) adversarial or fault‑injection task banks designed to raise baseline error prevalence (ambiguous intents, ordering-edge cases, protocol-specific pitfalls); (4) multi-model and sampling‑parameter sweeps to evaluate model- and sampling-sensitivity. Each of these modifications is compatible with the same paired estimand family but requires explicit preregistration of generation semantics and retry/repair budgets.

Threats to validity and operational boundaries. Internal validity: the single shared generation per intent and provider-default sampling (temperature = null) fix the generator distribution; sampling variation was recorded but not experimentally varied. Construct validity: emulator-executed faults are a conservative proxy for operational harm but omit live traffic, timing, and device-specific interactions present in production. External validity: the experiment used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini), one deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and a synthetic/emulated task bank; generalization to other models, vendor dialects, or production hardware is not supported. Conclusion validity: because baseline error prevalence was zero, the confirmatory design lacked power to demonstrate a verifier benefit in this execution. Residual contamination risk: exact‑match public-corpus checks were applied, but private-hosted-model training contamination cannot be entirely ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.

Operational implications and recommendations. Practitioners should view deterministic verifiers as layered risk controls rather than as a standalone cure. Demonstrating verifier value requires experiments that intentionally probe generator failure modes or permit verifier-triggered candidate changes. Where organizations deploy LLM-based NetOps tooling, we recommend instrumented A/B or pre-production trials with adversarial task samples, explicit repair budgets, multi-sample generation, and per-change emulation to measure true positive and false positive tradeoffs under realistic error rates.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) under shared_initial_candidate semantics to test whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and synthetic/emulated task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator faults and the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference = 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). This artifact-grounded null/ceiling outcome follows directly from the preregistered contract: when identical generated candidates produce no executed faults, a verifier cannot reduce executed faults under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Measuring verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires preregistered designs that permit independent or multiple generator samples, repair-enabled flows, adversarial task sets, and multi-model comparisons. All execution artifacts, validator traces, analysis logs, and the preregistration are archived in the evidence bundle to support replication and targeted follow‑on studies.

limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: the archived model configuration records temperature = null (provider default sampling semantics), leaving runtime sampling behavior as a recorded residual uncertainty.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
